A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

transference effects are evident in the social-cognitive processes of abused participants, with greater negativity in transference compared to control, but that these effects are moderated by the interpersonal context in ways that may be adaptive for abused participants.

transference is not only a social cognitive process that can be elicited experimentally, but it can have important implications for how individuals perceive and respond to others, particularly those with a history of abuse.

the transference effects we observed were more pronounced among participants with a history of parental abuse, particularly when the interpersonal situation was threatening, suggesting that the interpersonal difficulties experienced by abused individuals are at least partly a function of the transference process.

transference is a powerful social-cognitive process that can have important implications for interpersonal relations.
the effects of childhood maltreatment can be triggered by a single interaction with a stranger who resembles the abuser.
